issues.legal_issue: A property is not presumed to be joint family property merely because a joint Hindu family exists; the claimant must prove an adequate joint-family nucleus capable of supporting its acquisition before the burden shifts to the person asserting self-acquisition.
material_facts: The property in dispute had been purchased by a family member and was claimed by other family members as joint family property.

The family owned another property that was joint family property, but the claimants presented no evidence that it generated income or had a value sufficient to provide a nucleus for the purchase in dispute.
The claimants presented no other evidence establishing that the disputed property was joint family property.
The person who purchased the disputed property also presented no evidence of separate income.
issues.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a sufficient nucleus or otherwise prove that the disputed property was joint family property, so their claim to it failed; the purchaser’s failure to prove separate income did not shift the burden.
issues.legal_principle: Under Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, Srinivas Krishnarao Kango v. Narayan Devji Kango, Mudi Gowda Gowdappa Sankh v. Ram Chandra Ravagowda Sankh, Baikuntha Nath Paramanik v. Sashi Bhusan Pramanik, and Surendra Kumar v. Phoolchand, the existence of a joint family alone does not raise a presumption that a member’s property is joint. The person asserting joint-family character initially bears the burden. If that person proves an adequate joint-family nucleus from which the property could have been acquired, a presumption arises and the burden shifts to the person claiming self-acquisition. The adequacy of the nucleus depends on its nature, extent, and income. Mallesappa Bandeppa Desai v. Desai Mallappa, Achuthan Nair v. Chinnammu Amma, and Malappa Girimallappa Betgeri v. R. Yellappagouda Patil do not displace that rule where an adequate nucleus has not been established.

rule.if: partition_suit_claiming_joint_family_character and claimant_asserts_property_is_joint_family and not adequate_acquisition_nucleus_proved and not other_evidence_of_joint_family_character

predicates.partition_suit_claiming_joint_family_cha: A claimant seeks recognition of property as joint family property in a suit involving partition.
predicates.claimant_asserts_property_is_joint_famil: A claimant alleges that the disputed property belongs to the joint family.
predicates.adequate_acquisition_nucleus_proved: The claimant proves that joint-family property had sufficient value or income to provide a nucleus from which the disputed property could have been acquired.
predicates.other_evidence_of_joint_family_character: The claimant presents evidence, apart from an acquisition nucleus, that the disputed property is joint family property.

issues.definition: If a claimant in a partition suit alleges that property is joint family property but proves neither an adequate acquisition nucleus nor other evidence of its joint-family character, the claim to the property as joint family property fails.

issues.legal_issue: A member’s separate or self-acquired property becomes joint family property by blending only when the owner voluntarily places it into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon separate rights in it.
material_facts: The claimants argued that, even if the disputed property had originally been self-acquired, its owner had blended it with joint family property.
The claimants presented no evidence that the owner voluntarily placed the property into the common stock or clearly intended to abandon separate rights in it.
issues.conclusion: The disputed property could not be held to have been blended with joint family property because the claimants did not establish a clear intention to abandon the owner’s separate rights.
issues.legal_principle: A member’s separate or self-acquired property may acquire the character of joint family property if the owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock with the intention of abandoning separate rights. That intention must be clearly established. Joint use by family members, generosity in using income to support them, or failure to keep separate accounts does not by itself establish abandonment. The Court relied on Lakkireddi Chinna Venkata Reddy v. Lakkireddi Lakshamama and K.V. Narayanan v. K.V. Ranganadhan.

predicates.partition_suit_claiming_blending_of_sepa: A claimant seeks recognition of property as joint family property on the basis that its owner blended it with the family property.
predicates.owner_had_separate_property: The property was separate or self-acquired property of its owner.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_righ: Evidence establishes that the owner voluntarily placed the property into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon separate rights in it.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a partition suit relies on blending of the owner’s separate property but does not prove a clear intention to abandon separate rights, the property is not established as joint family property by blending.
